title: Molecular hydrogen formation on dust: The impact of gas-dust drift on formation efficiency
authors: Stefan Reissl, Simon C. O. Glover, Ralf S. Klessen, Liam S. Morrissey, Mordecai-Mark Mac Low
abstract: Molecular hydrogen is predominantly formed on dust-grain surfaces in the interstellar medium, where relative gas-dust motion can arise in dynamically active environments. While the dependence of H$_2$ formation on grain temperature and surface properties is well studied, the impact of gas-dust drift has received little attention. We investigate how gas-dust drift modifies H$_2$ formation, focusing on the competition between the drift-enhanced H-atom collision rate and reduced sticking at higher impact energies. We use an event-driven kinetic Monte Carlo model that follows individual H atoms on spherical silicate and carbonaceous grains, including adsorption, surface migration, thermal desorption, and Langmuir-Hinshelwood (LH) and Eley-Rideal (ER) reactions. Drift is described by a shifted Maxwellian velocity distribution, and we compare constant and impact-energy-dependent sticking probabilities. Drift produces increasingly anisotropic distributions of adsorbed H and H$_2$ formation across the grain surface. Assuming constant sticking, increasing drift enhances H$_2$ formation through the higher collision rate, with efficiencies up to $ε=0.3-0.4$. With energy-dependent sticking, strong drift instead suppresses formation on both materials, reducing efficiencies to $ε=0.01-0.03$. Carbonaceous grains remain efficient to higher dust temperatures than silicate grains. ER reactions dominate over most of the investigated parameter space and become increasingly important at strong drift as the reduced surface population suppresses LH reactions. Thus, enhanced collision rates under gas-dust drift do not necessarily increase H$_2$ formation. Models of dynamically active environments should account for both relative gas-dust velocities and their effects on sticking.
summary: This work models H2 formation on interstellar dust grains, critically incorporating the effect of systematic gas-dust drift into the chemical kinetics. Using a KMC simulation, the authors show that while increased collision rates might suggest higher formation, the energy dependence of sticking drastically suppresses the overall efficiency. This mandates that models for dynamic astrophysical environments must account for both relative gas-dust velocity and its impact on surface sticking.
main_problem: The paper investigates how systematic gas-dust drift modifies the efficiency of molecular hydrogen (H2) formation on interstellar dust grains.
main_result: Strong gas-dust drift suppresses H2 formation when sticking probability depends on impact energy, suggesting that simple collision rate enhancements are insufficient for accurate models of dynamic environments.
method: The authors employ an event-driven Kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) model to simulate individual H atoms interacting with spherical dust grains.
model_or_system: The system is the interstellar medium, modeling H2 formation on silicate and carbonaceous dust grains. The model incorporates adsorption, surface migration, thermal desorption, and both Langmuir-Hinshelwood (LH) and Eley-Rideal (ER) reaction channels.
key_observables: H2 formation efficiency (epsilon_H2), anisotropic distribution of adsorbed H and H2 on the grain surface.
important_parameters: Gas-dust drift velocity (characterized by a shifted Maxwellian distribution), sticking probability (constant vs. energy-dependent), and dust temperature.
main_assumptions: The model compares constant sticking assumptions against energy-dependent sticking, which is crucial for determining the correct physical regime.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the dependence of collision rate and sticking rate on dust temperature for various drift parameters, showing the mathematical framework for drift incorporation.
paper_structure: The paper develops the KMC framework to include drift via shifted Maxwellian sampling, compares results using constant vs. energy-dependent sticking, analyzes the dominance of ER over LH reactions under drift, and concludes with necessary revisions for modeling dynamic environments.
why_interesting: While focused on astrochemistry, the use of detailed KMC simulations to model surface reactions under non-equilibrium conditions (drift) provides a sophisticated example of applying advanced numerical techniques to complex, multi-scale physical processes.
